regions.labelEs: ¿QUÉ ES TODO ESTO DEL ALL YOUR BASE? ¿NO MURIÓ ESO COMO HACE CINCO AÑOS?

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the deliberately retained English title of the internet meme, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Del combines de and el and introduces the topic that the question is asking about.
Qué es todo esto de asks for an explanation of a noticed topic; de appears as del here because the translation treats the English meme title as taking el.
Hace comes before the five-year duration and turns it into a point measured backward from now.

regions.labelEs: FUE MI PRIMER MEME DE INTERNET, Y MI FAVORITO. OTROS SE HAN CANSADO DE ÉL, PERO YO NO.

applications.explanationEn: Han is the present helper for other people, and cansado is the completed-action form that follows it.
Se and han cansado form the plural present-perfect form of cansarse; de introduces él as what the tiredness is directed toward.
Él refers back to the masculine noun meme, so English uses “it” rather than “him.”
Yo names the contrasting person, and no lets the speaker leave the already-mentioned action unstated.
Así que introduces the result or consequence that follows.

regions.labelEs: ALGÚN DÍA, DENTRO DE UNAS DÉCADAS, LA GENTE LO HABRÁ OLVIDADO. SERÁ NUEVO OTRA VEZ. RETRO.

applications.explanationEn: Algún día names an unspecified future day.
Dentro de points forward from now, and unas décadas supplies the approximate delay.
Habrá is the future helper, and olvidado presents forgetting as complete by that later time.
Será keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds the third-person future ending -á.
Otra vez marks the state as returning or happening again.
The arrival is still in the future, so cuando is followed by llegue rather than a future-tense form.
Estaré adds the first-person future ending directly to the unchanged form estar.
O algo leaves the suggestion open instead of insisting on one exact alternative.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is a deliberately retained English quotation from the Zero Wing meme, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Todavía no is a complete short answer here because the action being discussed is already understood.

cards.questionEn: How can you ask what all the talk, activity, or fuss about a topic is?
cards.answerEn: Use ¿Qué es todo esto de ...? and name the topic after de.
cards.noteEn: This conversational frame asks for an explanation of something the speaker has noticed. De combines with el as del when the following topic takes that article.

example.es: ¿Qué es todo esto de la reunión sorpresa?
example.en: What is all this about the surprise meeting?

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

example.en: This is difficult.

cards.answerEn: about the (de + el, introducing a topic)
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After an expression that introduces a subject of discussion, de can mean “about,” so del introduces a masculine topic.

example.en: We talked about the new project.

cards.noteEn: Murió is the completed past form of morir for one person or thing.

example.es: La planta murió durante el invierno.
example.en: The plant died during the winter.

cards.noteEn: Before a number or amount of time, como can show that the amount is approximate rather than exact.

example.en: We waited about twenty minutes.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

example.en: I arrived two hours ago.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.

example.en: We met three months ago.

cards.noteEn: Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.answerEn: was (a completed past instance of ser)

cards.noteEn: Primero shortens to primer directly before a masculine singular noun: el primer libro. In other positions, use primero.

example.es: Es mi primer viaje a México.
example.en: It is my first trip to Mexico.

cards.answerEn: an early internet meme based on awkward English from the game Zero Wing
cards.noteEn: The best-known line is “All your base are belong to us.” “What you say!!” comes from the same badly translated game opening. The meme spread widely online around 2000–2001 and later became a marker of early-web nostalgia.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

example.en: I bought a history book.

cards.noteEn: Favorito can stand without a repeated noun when the noun is already understood: mi favorito means “my favorite one.”

example.es: De todos los libros, este es mi favorito.
example.en: Of all the books, this one is my favorite.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks cansarse, “to get tired”
cards.noteEn: Cansarse uses a small pronoun that changes with the person: me canso, te cansas, se cansa. Use se with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.en: They get tired of waiting.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets tired of or fed up with something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching pronoun and a form of cansarse, followed by de.
cards.noteEn: The pronoun changes with the person: me canso, te cansas, se cansa, nos cansamos. After de, use a noun or an unchanged action verb.

example.en: We get tired of arguing.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Cansado is the completed-action form of cansar. With a form of haber and cansarse de, cansado helps say that someone has become tired of something.

example.en: I have gotten tired of the noise.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; a required verb complement
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

example.en: I stopped smoking.

cards.answerEn: it (referring back to a masculine singular thing)
cards.noteEn: Él normally means “he” or “him,” but after a preposition it can also replace a masculine singular thing already named. English then uses “it.” Keep the accent to distinguish él from el, “the.”

example.es: El ruido es fuerte, pero me acostumbré a él.
example.en: The noise is loud, but I got used to it.

cards.promptEs: persona + sí/no con la acción ya entendida
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish say that one person does or does not do an already-mentioned action without repeating the action?
cards.answerEn: Name the person, then use sí or no; the earlier action can be left unstated.
cards.noteEn: Spanish often leaves out a verb or whole action when the listener can recover it from context. In Marta fue, pero yo no, yo no means that I did not go. For a positive contrast, use yo sí.

example.es: Luis cocina hoy, pero Ana no.
example.en: Luis is cooking today, but Ana isn't.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector

cards.noteEn: Esperar can mean either “to wait” or “to hope/expect.” When no hoped-for event or object follows, context can give it the simple meaning “to wait.”

example.en: I wait here.

cards.answerEn: some; some day/time (before a masculine noun)
cards.noteEn: Alguno shortens to algún directly before a masculine singular noun: algún día, algún libro.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “someday,” without naming a particular day?
cards.noteEn: This expression refers to an unspecified day, often in the future. Algún is the shortened form of alguno used before the masculine noun día.

example.en: Someday I will visit Chile.

cards.noteEn: Dentro de followed by a length of time looks forward from now: dentro de una semana means “in a week.”

example.en: I will return in an hour.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something will happen a certain amount of time from now?
cards.answerEn: Use dentro de before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Dentro de looks forward from the present: dentro de dos horas means “in two hours.” This differs from hace dos horas, which looks backward and means “two hours ago.”

example.es: El tren sale dentro de media hora.
example.en: The train leaves in half an hour.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes dentro de, “in”
cards.noteEn: When dentro de introduces a future delay, translate the two words together as “in.”

example.es: La película empieza dentro de diez minutos.
example.en: The movie starts in ten minutes.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.answerEn: will have (helper for a completed future action)
cards.noteEn: Habrá is the future form of the helper haber for one person or thing. Before a completed-action form such as terminado, it helps build “will have finished.”

example.en: Marta will have finished tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action will already be complete by a future point?
cards.answerEn: Use a future form of haber, then the action's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: The helper changes with the person: habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habréis, habrán. The following completed-action form stays unchanged: habrá llegado means “will have arrived.”

example.en: By Friday, we will have finished.

cards.noteEn: Olvidado is the completed-action form of olvidar, “to forget.” It follows a form of haber in perfect constructions.

example.en: I have forgotten his name.

cards.noteEn: Será is the future form of ser for one person or thing.

example.en: Tomorrow will be another day.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens again?
cards.noteEn: The expression literally uses “another time,” but natural English normally translates it as “again.”

example.en: Try it again.

cards.answerEn: retro; fashionable because it recalls the past
cards.noteEn: Retro describes a style, object, or idea that deliberately evokes an earlier time.

example.es: El café tiene una decoración retro.
example.en: The café has retro decor.

cards.promptEs: cuando + presente de subjuntivo para un hecho futuro
cards.questionEn: After cuando, how do you describe an event that has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use cuando followed by a present subjunctive form for the future event; put the main result in an ordinary future or command form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used here because the time of the future event is not yet a fact. For example, mover changes to mueva. Spanish does not normally put a future-tense form immediately after cuando in this pattern.

example.en: I will call you when I arrive.

cards.answerEn: arrives; comes (special form for a future event)
cards.noteEn: Llegue is a form of llegar used after connectors such as cuando or para que when the arrival has not happened yet. The written u keeps the hard g sound before e.

example.en: I will call you when I arrive.

cards.noteEn: Ese points to a masculine singular noun that is not presented as right next to the speaker. Feminine singular is esa.

example.en: I do not recognize that sound.

cards.noteEn: Estaré is the first-person future form of estar.

example.en: I will be at home tonight.

cards.noteEn: Hobby is an English loanword used in Spanish. A common Spanish alternative is afición or pasatiempo.

example.en: Photography is my hobby.

cards.questionEn: How can you make a suggestion less exact by adding “or something”?
cards.answerEn: Add o algo after the example or suggestion.
cards.noteEn: O algo leaves the alternatives open. It often makes an informal suggestion sound broad rather than precise.

example.es: Podemos tomar un café o algo.
example.en: We can have a coffee or something.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use todavía no before the action, or alone when the action is understood.
cards.noteEn: The Spanish order literally resembles “still not,” while natural English often uses “not yet.”

example.en: I am not ready yet.
